quote: people will pay only 28% more to protect all 57 wilderness areas in Ontario than one area
content: This garbles the essay's own earlier citation. "Scope Insensitivity" correctly places the 57 wilderness areas in four western US states; Ontario was the lakes study. The accompanying claim that "people will pay the same amount to save 50,000 lives as 5,000 lives" has no source. These are small errors, but they are the argument's evidential premises, restated from memory with the details changed.

quote: Two Israeli psychologists asked people to contribute to a costly life-saving treatment.
content: This is Kogut & Ritov (2005), relayed through a magazine article, and the essay leaves out the condition that changes its meaning. The effect appears when each subject sees only one recipient. When people compare the single child and the group of eight side by side, they give more to the group (Kogut & Ritov 2005b). Across studies the identified-victim effect is small: a meta-analysis found an average effect of about r = 0.05 (Lee & Feeley 2016). The "worst case of scope insensitivity" is a modest effect that disappears when people get a comparison to multiply with.

quote: It is a general principle that Bayesians see no difference between the long-run answer and the short-run answer
content: This is not a principle of Bayesian decision theory, and there are well-known cases where the two come apart. Maximizing expected wealth and maximizing long-run growth (the Kelly criterion) recommend different bets. Samuelson (1979) insisted, famously in words of one syllable, that an expected-utility maximizer should not maximize the mean log of wealth just because the years to act are long. The ergodicity literature makes the same point for multiplicative gambles (Peters 2019). The long run is not a neutral intuition pump; it smuggles in an assumption about aggregation.

quote: Anyway, I accept 3, 5, 6, and 7, but not 4
content: Statement 7 says that for any harms A and B, some tiny probability of A is preferable to a certain B. Combine it with unbounded utility, which "Newcomb's Problem" endorses, and you get fanaticism: tiny probabilities of astronomically large outcomes dominate every decision. That is the structure of Pascal's mugging. Philosophers have shown that avoiding fanaticism requires giving up something the author also accepts (Beckstead & Thomas 2023), and some accept fanaticism outright (Wilkinson 2022). The essay accepts the premises without noticing where they lead, and the author's own Pascal's-mugging post shows he found the destination unacceptable.

quote: You don’t conclude that utilities must be expressed using hyper-real numbers. Because the lower tier would simply vanish in any equation.
content: The lower tier of a lexical ordering doesn't vanish. It decides every case where the upper tier is tied, and in ordinary life most choices don't touch the upper tier at all. The essay's reply is that once probabilities are included, every act carries some tiny risk to life, so the upper tier is never tied. That shows lexical views are impractical when combined with a precise probability for every risk. It doesn't show they are incoherent, and non-Archimedean utility theory is a consistent mathematical structure (Fishburn 1974). "Impractical given my other commitments" and "irrational" are different claims.
